The Lobby That Buys Elections, Cheaper Every Cycle

Two years ago Cori Bush stood in front of AIPAC and promised to "tear your kingdom down." On Tuesday, the kingdom sent the bill again — just a smaller one this time. It still cashed the check.

Wesley Bell, the man who unseated her in 2024, beat her again in their rematch — this time by roughly 45 points. Not a nail-biter. A rout.

Here's the arithmetic of that rout. In 2024, AIPAC's super PAC spent about $9 million tearing Bush down. This time, roughly $2 to $3 million did the job. Same outcome. A third of the price. Someone in that lobby's finance department deserves a bonus for efficiency.

Bush had genuine tailwind this cycle. She was one of the first members of Congress to call Israel's war in Gaza a "genocide", and Democratic voters have been drifting toward exactly that framing. 

In June, Democratic Socialists of America-backed challengers ousted three sitting Democrats, including Adriano Espaillat, chairman of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, who lost to a 32-year-old community organizer by three points. The socialist wave was real. It just broke somewhere else.

Missouri's 1st District is safely Democratic. Bell's actual November opponent doesn't exist yet in any meaningful sense — he's already won the only election that counted. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the Congressional Black Caucus PAC lined up behind him anyway, because nothing says "grassroots energy" like the entire party leadership showing up to make sure a safe seat stays exactly as safe as it already was.

Bush's allies spent under $200,000 total. AIPAC's people alone outspent her tenfold on advertising and still had budget left for coffee.

So which is the actual story here — that a progressive movement is rising inside the Democratic Party, or that it's rising everywhere except the districts a well-funded lobby has decided to keep?

ONE BILL WILL NOT DEFINE THE ENTIRE MARKET.

The Crypto CLARITY Act remains one of the most important regulatory developments for the US digital asset industry.

The Senate Banking Committee advanced the legislation in May by a bipartisan 15–9 vote.

But the bill has not yet passed the full Senate and has not become law.

At the same time, the regulatory process is not standing still.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins has said that the Commission’s 2026 agenda includes:

• clearer rules for crypto capital formation
• bringing more digital asset products onshore
• custody guidance
• rules for trading tokenized securities onchain

This creates two parallel processes.

Congress can establish a permanent statutory framework and define agency authority.

Regulators can interpret existing laws and develop rules inside the authority they already have.

Those processes are connected.

They are not interchangeable.

Agency rulemaking cannot automatically replace legislation.

Legislation cannot implement itself without detailed regulatory work.

For digital asset companies, the important questions are therefore broader than:

“Will the CLARITY Act pass this week?”

They include:

• What rules are already changing?
• Which agency currently has authority?
• What requires new legislation?
• Which obligations will depend on future rulemaking?
• How long will implementation take after passage?

A headline can create momentum.

A functioning market structure requires:

- law

- rules

- implementation

- enforcement

Legislation defines the architecture.
Regulation turns it into an operating system.

For 9 years, I was a senior actuary at one of the top five health insurance companies in the United States. My job was simple: predict when people will get sick, how long they will stay sick, and how much it will cost. I built the models. I ran the numbers. I was very, very good at it.

In early 2021, my models started breaking.

Not slightly. Catastrophically.

A specific subset of policyholders — all classified as "terminal" or "high-cost chronic" — were suddenly dropping off our claims database. These were people with Stage 4 cancers, advanced organ failure, degenerative neurological conditions. People who, according to every actuarial model ever built, should have been filing $300,000 to $1.2 million in claims annually until death.

Instead, their claims just... stopped.

⟁

At first, I assumed data error. I ran the audit. No error. 

Then I assumed death. I cross-referenced the Social Security Death Index. They weren't dead.

Then I assumed they switched insurers. I checked the industry-wide shared risk database. They hadn't switched. They simply had no medical claims anywhere in the system. Zero. As if they had become perfectly healthy overnight.

Between January 2021 and December 2023, I identified exactly 1,247 policyholders across our book who fit this pattern. Terminal diagnosis, followed by complete cessation of all medical activity. Not death. Not hospice. Not alternative care. Nothing.

⟁

I flagged it to my department head. He told me to "re-categorize them as data anomalies and move on." I didn't move on.

I started mapping the 1,247 cases geographically. What I found made my stomach drop.

83% of them lived within 60 miles of a known military installation. Not random bases — specific ones. The same 14 facilities kept appearing. Fort Detrick. Wright-Patterson. Nellis. China Lake. Dugway. The pattern was undeniable.

I then cross-referenced their last known medical appointments before the claims stopped. In 91% of cases, their final civilian appointment included a referral code I had never seen before: "MRT-7 / GOV-AUTH."

Medical Regeneration Transfer. Government Authorized.

I presented it to the VP of Risk Assessment. He read it in silence. Then he said: "You need to understand something. There are clients we insure who are not supposed to get better. And there are clients who are selected to get better. Your job is to model the first group. The second group does not exist in your spreadsheet. Do you understand?"

I understood. I understood that 1,247 people were cured of terminal illness using technology that my company — and every insurance company — knows about but will never acknowledge. Because if the public knew a cure existed, the entire $4.5 trillion healthcare industry collapses overnight.

⟁

I resigned in March 2024. I kept copies of everything.

The technology is real. The cures are real. The numbers don't lie. And now that the declassification has begun, every actuarial table in the country is about to become obsolete.
